subject: Critical Thinking
title: The Narrative Fallacy: Stories Beat Statistics
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Narrative Fallacy: Stories Beat Statistics usable.

hook.text: One crying child on TV raises millions. A statistic of 100,000 deaths raises nothing. Stories beat numbers every time.

buildup.text: The narrative fallacy: we prefer stories to data because our brains are wired for narrative, not statistics.

discovery.text: Nassim Taleb: we construct stories after the fact to explain events that were actually random or multi-causal.

twist.text: Biographies of successful people create false narratives: 'She succeeded because of grit.' Ignoring luck, timing, &.

climax.text: Stories make sense of chaos. That's their power — and their danger. Sense-making isn't truth-finding.

punchline.text: A good story isn't good evidence. It's just memorable.

quiz.question: What is the narrative fallacy?
options: We prefer narratives over data and construct false causal stories
Statistics are more convincing than stories

details.summary: The narrative fallacy is the human tendency to construct coherent stories from random events and then believe the stories are true. We prefer a compelling narrative over messy statistical reality.
details.whyItMatters: Stories feel true because our brains are wired for narrative, but this wiring causes us to impose false patterns on random data and mistake explanation for prediction.
takeaways: Humans are compulsive storytellers who impose patterns on randomness
A good story feels more convincing than solid statistics
Nassim Taleb popularized the term in 'The Black Swan'

faq.question: Why do stories feel more convincing than statistics to most people?
faq.answer: Stories activate empathy, memory, and emotion simultaneously. Statistics engage abstract reasoning, which is effortful and less engaging. Our brains evolved to learn from stories, not spreadsheets.

faq.question: How does the narrative fallacy affect how we understand history?
faq.answer: We construct neat causal chains to explain historical events that were actually driven by randomness, contingency, and multiple interacting causes. The clean narrative replaces messy reality with false certainty.
